Chapter 4: Embracing Influence and Sharing Power in the Relationship
Picture a marriage—not as a tug-of-war for control—but as a real partnership, where both people genuinely feel heard, respected, and empowered.
One of the biggest signs of a happy marriage? It’s when each partner is willing to accept influence from the other. That means you’re both open to each other’s ideas, feelings, and perspectives. You make decisions together—not just on your own.
But let’s be honest—sometimes, power struggles sneak in. Maybe one partner resists input, or insists on having the final say. When that happens, it can create resentment and distance, chipping away at the sense of teamwork that every strong marriage needs.
On the other hand, when you share power and influence, you’re not just resolving conflicts—you’re building mutual respect. You’re showing that you value each other’s voice.
Now, accepting influence doesn’t mean you give up your own needs or opinions. It’s really about compromise, and seeing your relationship as a team effort. Think of it like a dance—sometimes you lead, sometimes you follow, and you’re always adjusting your steps together.
So, how can you actually embrace influence in your day-to-day life?
Try listening actively, especially when you don’t agree right away. Ask for your partner’s input before making decisions that affect you both. And be willing to adjust your plans if your partner has different needs.
For example, say you’re figuring out how to spend a weekend. Maybe you’d love to stay home, while your partner wants to get out and explore. Instead of one person winning, talk it out. Maybe you can alternate activities, or find a plan that makes you both happy.
This approach really matters when conflict pops up. If you’re both open to influence, disagreements don’t have to turn into power struggles. Instead, they become chances to collaborate and solve problems together. Even when compromise is tough, just listening and considering each other’s perspective can build goodwill and understanding.
Of course, your background and culture might shape how you think about power and influence. Maybe you learned that giving in means you’re weak, or that compromise is somehow a loss. Overcoming those patterns takes self-awareness and a real commitment to your relationship’s health.
In the end, sharing power is really about honoring your partnership. When both of you feel your voice matters, you’re more likely to invest in the relationship—and to support each other’s growth.
That sense of equality and respect? It’s what makes a marriage truly lasting and fulfilling.
